author: Morgan Busby
title: Lieutenant Governor candidate Ryan McLaren visits Woodstock while on the campaign trail | The Vermont Standard
text:
Ryan McLaren, one of the two principal candidates seeking the Democratic nomination for Vermont’s lieutenant governor in the upcoming August 11 primary, visited Hartford and Woodstock on a campaign swing last Friday.
As he does in every community he visits, McLaren met with first responders in Hartford in the morning and Woodstock in the afternoon, sandwiching a stop at the daily Tribou Park protest in between during the noon hour. It was the 462nd consecutive day of the Woodstock vigil, and about 20 people were on hand to converse with McLaren about his life, his commitment to public service, and his positions on key issues affecting average Vermonters, such as education transformation, housing accessibility, and the soaring inequities in health care.
The Standard caught up with McLaren and his campaign manager, Molly Moore, at the Tribou Park gathering and then headed off to lunch and an hour-long chat with the candidate. The focus of the discussion was more about the kind of person McLaren is and what makes him tick, rather than his positions on the most pressing issues of the day. That said, McLaren did speak several times about the intricate interconnectedness of the education, housing, and health care crises that are vexing so many people, both locally and statewide.
At his core, McLaren said, he’s dedicated his life to community and public service largely due to the influence of his parents and his blue-collar upbringing. He speaks of his parents, Rob and Diane Noel McLaren, with deep-seated love, appreciation, and admiration for the values they instilled in him.
“The issues that are so personal to me when I talk about why I’m running for office, it’s all because of my parents,” he explained. “My parents gave me a life and my siblings a life that I’m really grateful for — they worked their butts off raising three kids in a 900-square-foot house in Essex Junction, having not gone to college themselves, but working blue-collar jobs to make ends meet,” McLaren added. “We had help along the way — I grew up on Dr. Dinosaur, so we didn’t go broke when I got sick, and I grew up on WIC and food stamps, so we had help when we needed food. All of that fit together to make my life possible. There’s the infrastructure of opportunity that was available to me through my parents’ hard work and community investment that gave me the life I have today — and I’m really grateful for it.
“So much of what motivates me in public service is that sense that every kid like me can thrive if they’re given the opportunity, given the resources,” the candidate continued. “But it’s so much harder today than it ever was. The other thing I think a lot about with my parents is that so much of my sense of public service is tied to what they did. It was never political: my dad coached every team I was ever on, and my parents were involved in everything I was ever involved in. That helped build a sense of community around me and my siblings. We had other people involved in our lives, too — other parents who drove me to hockey games when my parents couldn’t. There was this very real sense of community investment in my life that I just feel a lot of gratitude for,” he offered.
“There’s this sense of obligation to make sure we carry on with those values — and that what was possible for me is possible for other kids,” McLaren added. “I want to lower the ladder: my generation cannot be the last generation where working people can aspire to own a home, send their kids to college, and raise a family in Vermont. That would be a tragedy. But we’re reaching a breaking point on that, which is what’s motivating us so much right now,” McLaren offered.
For more on this, please see our May 21 edition of the Vermont Standard.
